claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be synthesized and maintained as a high-temperature single-phase BCC alloy.
Phase stability during cooling from the high-temperature BCC state is governed by competition between an Al-induced thermodynamic drive for chemical ordering and diffusion kinetics.
Al favors chemical ordering in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Slow cooling permits sufficient atomic rearrangement to form nanoscale ordered domains.
Formation of nanoscale ordered domains destabilizes the homogeneous BCC structure.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and kinetically traps a metastable BCC phase.
The proposed controlled comparison is between identical samples subjected to slow cooling or isothermal aging and samples subjected to rapid quenching.
The experiments should use an inert atmosphere and identical initial microstructures.
The cooling treatments must span a temperature range in which atomic diffusion is active.
The structural mediator is nucleation and growth of Al-induced nanoscale ordered domains or clusters within the BCC matrix.
Chemical ordering lowers the free energy of the alloy relative to the high-temperature homogeneous BCC state.
Slowly cooled samples should show superlattice reflections and ordered domains relative to rapidly quenched samples.
Rapidly quenched samples should remain a uniform BCC phase.
The rapidly quenched alloy is the baseline representing the retained high-temperature homogeneous BCC state.
The proposed mechanism applies within a thermal regime below the BCC stability limit in which diffusion is activated.
Extreme thermal gradients or substantial composition changes may invalidate the mechanism by altering diffusion kinetics.
The onset temperature, kinetics, and detectable extent of ordering may vary with minor changes in thermal history and processing.
A lack of statistically significant phase or ordering differences between slowly cooled and rapidly quenched samples would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says cooling rate is the only experimental variable, but permits isothermal aging as an alternative to slow cooling. Aging introduces an additional hold temperature and duration, so it is not a cooling-rate-only comparison.
